The data in this package comes from other organizations, under several different licenses, and the numbers a model produces depend on which version of which source it used. This page shows how to find out where a dataset came from, how to cite it, and how to make an analysis reproducible.

## Attribution travels with the data

Every dataset records its source, URL, license and citation, along with when and by which package version it was built. `provenance()` shows it, for fetched datasets too, without downloading anything:

```{python}
import starsim_data as ssd

ssd.provenance('prem2021')
```

The same record is attached to every dataframe `load()` returns:

```{python}
deaths = ssd.load('kenya', which='deaths')
deaths.attrs['provenance'].citation
```

```{python}
deaths.attrs['location'], deaths.attrs['dataset']
```

Provenance for every dataset is available at once:

```{python}
sorted(ssd.provenance().keys())
```

## Licenses

The data is not covered by this package's MIT license; each dataset keeps its original license.

```{python}
ssd.list_datasets(detailed=True)[['dataset', 'access', 'license']]
```

[NOTICE.md](https://github.com/starsimhub/starsim_data/blob/main/NOTICE.md) has the full attribution text, and the `licenses/` folder in the repository has the original license texts.

GADM boundaries are licensed for non-commercial use only. This package never uses GADM unless you ask for it by name, and never redistributes anything derived from it; if you download it, following its terms is up to you. See [Data sources](datasources.qmd#gadm).

## Downloaded data

Data downloaded from its original publisher (with `download()` and the `download_*()` functions) is saved on your computer, along with a note of where and when it was downloaded. `ssd.cache_info()` lists everything saved so far:

```python
ssd.cache_info()
#   file                                              size       url                            downloaded
#   wpp/WPP2024_Demographic_Indicators_Medium.csv.gz  16.557 MB  https://population.un.org/...  2026-08-07T19:31:36+00:00
```

Dataframes returned by `fetch()` and `download()` carry the same information in `df.attrs['provenance']`.

## Making an analysis reproducible

Four steps, most important first.

**Pin the package version.** Everything bundled or fetched is the same for everyone using a given version of the package, so pinning the version (for example `starsim_data==2.2.0` in your requirements file) fixes the demographics, the contact matrices and the node table together.

**Pin the WPP revision.** `load(..., revision=2024)` fixes the UN WPP release. Without it, `load()` uses the most recent revision in the package, so a future version could change what your script reads. Older revisions are kept when new ones are added, so a pinned revision stays available.

**Record what was downloaded.** Data downloaded from its original publisher depends on when you downloaded it, since publishers revise their files. Saving the output of `ssd.cache_info()` with your results records what you used and when.

**Record the boundary source.** Different boundary sources don't always divide a country up the same way, so two analyses that used different sources aren't directly comparable. The source is in `nodes.source` and in the provenance of any downloaded boundaries.

If you're curious how the bundled data is built from its sources, and how that is checked, see [Building the data](building-the-data.qmd).

## Citation

Cite the original sources, not just this package: UN World Population Prospects 2024 for the demographics, the relevant paper for each contact-matrix source you use, and UNOCHA and geoBoundaries for the node table. The citations are available in Python:

```{python}
{name: ssd.provenance(name).citation[:80] + '...'
 for name in ['deaths', 'prem2021', 'mistry2021']}
```

[NOTICE.md](https://github.com/starsimhub/starsim_data/blob/main/NOTICE.md) gives the complete text for each source.
